solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Oil and gel unit supply for old chopper

indicators.note: read as the adverb from supple, it means bendily or flexibly, so the letters are bent into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A shopping note about supplying oil and gel to keep an antique axe in working order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Supply' looks like a verb meaning provide, but it is the adverb of supple: the three words are bent into GUILLOTINE.
explanation.definitionFit: The guillotine was the beheading machine of revolutionary France, a historical device that literally chopped off heads.

clue.text: A line to break open Black… just castle!

indicators.note: breaking something open lets another thing push inside it, so one part is lodged within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
L is the standard abbreviation for line
B is the abbreviation for black, as on pencils
just in the sense of fair and upright

explanation.surface: A chess-like instruction: send a line through Black's defences and just take the castle.
explanation.walkthrough: A and L go inside the outer pair of B and MORAL, between them. Balmoral is the royal family's castle in the Scottish Highlands.
explanation.definitionFit: Balmoral is a specific example of a castle, the Scottish estate used by the British monarch as a summer residence.

clue.text: Goat-like female some ordinary Tasmanian rejected

indicators.note: some means only a part, so the letters are a portion of the neighbouring words
something rejected is sent back, so the letters are taken in the opposite direction

blocks.note: the tail of ordinary joined to the start of Tasmanian

explanation.surface: A wildlife note: a goat-like female of an everyday Tasmanian species was turned away.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run backwards across 'ordinarY TASmanian'. A satyra is the rare female form of satyr.
explanation.definitionFit: Satyrs in Greek myth were woodland spirits with goat features, and a satyra is the female counterpart of that creature.

clue.text: Banker’s bottom contrary vicar grabbed by shocked bride

indicators.note: contrary means facing the opposite way, so the letters run backwards
something shocked is jolted out of its normal state, so the letters are scrambled
what is grabbed ends up held inside the grabber

blocks.note: Rev is the short form of Reverend, a vicar's title
taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A wedding scandal: the bride is appalled when an awkward vicar gets hold of her bottom.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banker' is a crossword favourite for a river, the thing with banks, so this is not about money or anatomy.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is something that has banks, and the bed is the lowest part of its channel, so the river's floor is its bottom.

clue.text: Infuriating item seen in left-wing paper

blocks.note: red is the colour of socialism and the left
a rag is a scornful word for a newspaper

explanation.surface: Something maddening has turned up in a socialist newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen in' suggests one part inside another, but here it only joins definition to wordplay. A red rag is said to enrage a bull.
explanation.definitionFit: Anything that provokes fury is called a red rag, from the idea of a matador's cloth goading a bull into charging.

clue.text: Unkind bloke filled with animosity at the front

indicators.note: a vessel filled with something holds it inside
the front of a word is its opening letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: a bloke is a man
animosity is enmity, whose opening letter is E

explanation.surface: A spiteful man, brimming with hostility towards whoever is in front of him.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letter comes from a synonym, ENMITY, not from 'animosity' itself, so taking its A leads nowhere. The E sits inside MAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Calling someone mean describes cruel or spiteful behaviour towards others, the same quality as being unkind.

clue.text: One with brass in bar knocked back drop of Asti

indicators.note: a drink knocked back is downed, but read literally it is pushed back the way it came
a drop is the smallest amount, so only the first letter is taken

blocks.note: bar and but both mean except
the first letter of the Italian sparkling wine

explanation.surface: A wealthy drinker in a bar knocks back the last drop of Asti, an Italian sparkling wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' looks like money and 'bar' and 'knocked back' look like drinking. Bar as a preposition means except, as does but.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the deepest member of the brass section of an orchestra, so it is one instrument among the brass.

clue.text: I screamed out on taking bath ultimately

definitions.text: I screamed out on taking bath ultimately

indicators.note: out can mean disordered or not in place, so the letters are reorganised
ultimately means in the end, so only the last letter is used

indicators.text: I screamed out on taking bath ultimately
indicators.note: the whole sentence is the famous story of the speaker leaping from the tub with a cry

blocks.note: taken as written
the final letter of bath

explanation.surface: Someone recalls yelling as they finally got into the bath.
explanation.walkthrough: The rearranged letters plus the end of 'bath' give the Greek scientist, and the whole clue is his own boast: he shouted 'Eureka!' on getting into a bath.
explanation.definitionFit: Legend says the Greek mathematician noticed water displacement while bathing and ran through Syracuse shouting Eureka, exactly the scene described.

clue.text: Bats chase spiders around new hole in the wall

indicators.note: around means encircling, so one piece is held among the other letters
bats is slang for crazy, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for new

explanation.surface: Bats hunt spiders around a fresh crack in a wall, a nature-documentary moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bats' wants to be the flying animals but it is the signal word, meaning mad. 'Hole in the wall' is British slang for an ATM.
explanation.definitionFit: Britons call a street cash machine a hole in the wall because it is set into the outside wall of a bank.

clue.text: Jesus is black Briton, according to a Yank…

blocks.note: B is the abbreviation for black
limey is American slang for a British person

explanation.surface: A provocative claim that Jesus was a black Briton, as told by an American.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jesus' is not the person but the exclamation of surprise. Limey comes from the lime juice once given to British sailors.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words are mild British exclamations of astonishment, used interchangeably as expletives when something is shocking.

clue.text: …highly critical about wife’s blasphemy

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so one piece goes round another

blocks.note: searing criticism is scorching and severe
W is the abbreviation for wife

explanation.surface: Continuing from the previous clue, someone fiercely condemns a wife's profane remark.
explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis ties this to the previous clue's exclamation, which is itself an instance of the answer. W slips in after the first letter of SEARING.
explanation.definitionFit: Blasphemy is irreverent talk about God, and taking the Lord's name in vain is a common form of profane language.

clue.text: Servant tucking into fruit is a greedy guts

indicators.note: to tuck into is to go inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a gourd is a hard-skinned fruit
a manservant is a man

explanation.surface: A servant scoffing fruit is labelled a glutton.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tucking into' suggests eating, which fits the greedy surface, but it means going inside. 'Greedy guts' is British slang for a glutton.
explanation.definitionFit: A gourmand is someone who eats to excess, so the word names a glutton rather than a refined connoisseur.

clue.text: Promotional ploy by head of fell-walkers: “Take a hike!”

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: BOGOF stands for buy one get one free, a supermarket offer
the opening letter of fell-walkers

explanation.surface: The leader of a hill-walking group launches a marketing gimmick with the slogan 'Take a hike!'.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Take a hike!' sounds like a walking slogan but means go away. BOGOF is British shop jargon for buy one get one free.
explanation.definitionFit: Both are rude dismissals telling someone to go away; 'bog off' is mild British slang with the same force.

clue.text: American agent helping to protect European alliance

indicators.note: to protect something is to wrap it up safely, so one piece holds another

blocks.note: a fed is a US federal agent, such as an FBI officer
a helping or portion of food
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A US agent is helping to guard a European alliance.
explanation.walkthrough: The joined agent and helping together act as the protector, so the European letter lands where they meet. A fed is American slang for an FBI officer.
explanation.definitionFit: A federation is a union of states or groups joined for common purposes, which makes it a kind of alliance.

clue.text: Sick and embarrassed about Tory Party being rash

indicators.note: about here means concerning, so the colour word is attached to what it is about, coming after it

blocks.note: ill means sick
Con is short for Conservative, the Tory party
a party or side in a dispute
embarrassment makes the face go red

explanation.surface: A political jab: the Tories are sickly and red-faced about their own hasty decisions.
explanation.walkthrough: The colour for embarrassment comes last although it is read early: it is the feeling about the party, so it follows it. Con is the usual short form of Conservative.
explanation.definitionFit: A rash action is done without proper thought, which is exactly what an ill-considered one is.

clue.text: Old letter containing oversights?

blocks.note: O is the abbreviation for old
a missive is a formal word for a letter

explanation.surface: An ancient letter full of mistakes and gaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old letter' reads as one idea, an antique missive, but splits into O and the word for a letter. The question mark flags a rare adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Omissive describes something marked by leaving things out, and an oversight is a thing accidentally left out.

clue.text: When conservative in conference becomes roguish

indicators.note: in places one thing inside another

blocks.note: as and when both mean at the time that
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a rally is a large political gathering

explanation.surface: A buttoned-up delegate turns mischievous at a party conference.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Conservative' looks like a politician at the conference, but it only supplies its abbreviation, slipped with 'when' inside the gathering's word.
explanation.definitionFit: A rascal is a mischievous rogue, so rascally behaviour has the same impish dishonesty as roguish behaviour.

clue.text: One after leaders to negotiate enfranchisement with China?

definitions.text: One after leaders to negotiate enfranchisement with China?

indicators.note: leaders are the front-runners, so the opening letters of the next words are taken
after means following, so one piece is placed at the end

indicators.text: One after leaders to negotiate enfranchisement with China?
indicators.note: the whole sentence also describes a citizen of a Himalayan land bordering China seeking a deal

blocks.note: opening letters of the two words
china means mate in Cockney rhyming slang (china plate, mate), and a mate is a pal
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: Someone, perhaps from a small neighbouring state, wants to bargain with Beijing over voting rights.
explanation.walkthrough: 'China' looks like the country but it is the rhyming slang. The whole clue doubles as a hint: Nepal borders China.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nepali is a citizen of Nepal, the Himalayan state on China's southern border, the person imagined in the scene.

clue.text: A cessation of war broadcast to every person

indicators.note: a broadcast is heard rather than read, so the sound of the word matters, not its spelling

blocks.note: taken as written
the end of fighting is peace

explanation.surface: An armistice is announced over the airwaves to the whole population.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' suggests the ceasefire is announced on radio, but it signals the sound swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Apiece is an adverb meaning for each one, as in 'five pounds apiece', so it fits 'to every person'.

clue.text: Old work retrospective bound to get publicity

indicators.note: retrospective means looking back, so the letters face the other way

blocks.note: an ex is a former one
op is short for opus, a work
bound to happen means sure to happen

explanation.surface: A gallery's retrospective of an artist's early work is certain to draw press attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Retrospective' looks like an exhibition, but it turns the short form of opus around. 'To get' links the pieces to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting exposure means being seen widely in the media, so it is the attention that publicity provides.

clue.text: Unhealthy-looking cakes close to butter tart?

indicators.note: to cake is to coat thickly, so one piece is covered by another
the close of a word is its end, so its final letter is used

blocks.note: pasty means pale and sickly
the final letter of butter

explanation.surface: Pale, sad-looking cakes sit next to a buttery tart in a bakery window.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cakes' looks like baked goods, fitting the bakery surface, but it is a verb: coats over. The question mark marks a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A tart is one kind of baked item made from pastry, so the definition is an example, flagged with a question mark.

clue.text: Pair set off with son for lengthy perambulations

indicators.note: off can mean gone bad or out of order, so the letters are knocked out of place

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written
S is the abbreviation for son

explanation.surface: A couple head out with their boy on long walks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Set off' reads as a phrase meaning depart, but only 'off' is the signal; 'set' joins the letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: Traipses are long, tiring walks taken wearily, so they are drawn-out strolls about the place.

clue.text: Bust of king female attendant originally nicked

indicators.note: nicked means stolen, so the original or opening letter is taken away

blocks.note: R is Rex, Latin for king
a maid is a female servant

explanation.surface: A statue of a king and his lady-in-waiting has been stolen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bust' looks like a sculpture, but it is the police sense, and 'nicked' plays on arrest too.
explanation.definitionFit: A police bust is a surprise swoop on premises to make arrests or seize goods, which is what a raid is.

clue.text: Quiet worker first to yodel a salty tune?

indicators.note: first means the opening position, so only the starting letter is used

blocks.note: sh is the sound used to ask for quiet
a worker ant is the standard crossword worker
the opening letter of yodel

explanation.surface: A shy labourer is the first to yodel a slightly rude song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Salty' suggests a risqué song, but here it means of the sea: a shanty is a sailors' work song.
explanation.definitionFit: A sea shanty is a song sung by sailors at work, and an old sailor is called a salt.

clue.text: You might say 8 records I’ve given a remix

indicators.note: saying something is speaking it, so the sound counts rather than the spelling

blocks.note: a person who records a cover version of discs

explanation.surface: A DJ boasts about remixing some old records.
explanation.walkthrough: 8 is ARCHIMEDES. Someone who has remixed records could be called a disc coverer, which spoken aloud runs together into the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Archimedes is famed for finding the principle of buoyancy, so he is an example of a scientist who found something new.

clue.text: State the Spanish invaded by Asia’s western tip

indicators.note: an invaded territory has an intruder inside its borders
in an across word the west end is the left, so the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: los is a Spanish word for the
the opening letter of Asia

explanation.surface: A historical picture of a Spanish state being invaded from Asia's western edge.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening letter of 'Asia' goes inside the Spanish article.
explanation.definitionFit: Laos is a landlocked country in Southeast Asia, so it is an example of a sovereign nation or state.
